en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
6. The Exposition of the Question of the Young Man Upasīva:
"Alone, Sakka, I [cross] the great flood," said the Venerable Upasīva.
I am unable to cross over without a support;
O All-Seeing One, tell me the object of focus by relying upon which I might cross this flood.
"I am alone, Sakka, like one in a great flood.
"Alone" means that I have no second person as my companion, nor do I have a second doctrine as my companion—
by relying on which person or by relying on which doctrine I might cross over and transcend the great flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
"I shall leap over, transcend, and pass beyond. He is called Sakka because he is capable;
furthermore, the Blessed One is called Sakka because he went forth from the Sakyan clan.
Alternatively, he is called "Sakka" because he is wealthy, possessing great riches and being affluent.
These are his riches, namely:

the wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of moral shame, the wealth of moral dread, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of the foundations of mindfulness... [and so forth].
The treasure of Nibbāna.
Because he is enriched with these many treasures and jewels, Sakka is called "the wealthy one," "the one of great wealth," and "the possessor of riches.

Alternatively, Sakka is so called because he is powerful (*pahu*), capable (*visavī*), self-sufficient (*alamatto*), brave (*sūro*), heroic (*vīro*), resolute (*vikkanto*), fearless (*abhīrū*), undaunted (*achambhī*), unafraid (*anutrāsī*), not fleeing (*apalāyī*), having abandoned fear and terror (*pahīnabhayabheravo*), and being free from horripilation (*vigatalomahaṁso*). Thus he is called Sakka.

“Alone, Sakka, am I in this great flood,” said the Venerable Upasīva. “Itti” (thus) refers to the connection between words... [etc.]... The Venerable Upasīva said: “Alone, Sakka, am I in this great flood. “Thus” (*iti*) is a particle used for quoting; it indicates that what follows is the very speech uttered by the speaker. It is a term for connecting words (*padasandhi*). ... [and so on] ... “Venerable” (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment... [etc.
...“Upasīva” is the name of that brahmin... [etc. ...the utterance “thus”—this is how he is called “Venerable Upasīva.”
"I am not dependent; I am unable to cross over.

Here, "not dependent" means that being neither dependent on a person nor dependent on a phenomenon, I am not able, not capable, not competent, and not empowered to cross over, to transcend, and to traverse the great flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
"To transcend" means to pass beyond.
"I am unable to cross over, being without support"—O All-Seeing One, tell me the object!
Tell me, declare, show, point out, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and explain the object, the support, the basis, and the decisive support.
"Samantacakkhu" means all-seeing vision; it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
The Blessed One is endowed with, fully endowed with, has attained, fully attained, is possessed of, fully possessed of, and is equipped with that omniscient knowledge.
There is nothing whatsoever in this world that is unseen by him.
And furthermore, that which is unknown and ought to be known— whatever is to be understood,
all that the Tathāgata has directly realized; therefore, he is the All-Seeing One.
"Tell me the object, O All-Seeing One:
depending upon what might one cross over this flood?

"Depending upon what": depending upon which person or depending upon which Dhamma, one might cross over, transcend, surmount, pass beyond, and overcome the great flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
"Relying on which I might cross over this flood"—
with that in mind, that brahmin said:
"Alone, Sakka, I [cross] the great flood."
(Thus spoke the Venerable Upasīva:
"I am unable to cross over without support;
tell me an object of focus, O All-Seeing One."
“Relying on which one might cross this flood?
“Perceiving nothingness, mindful,” said the Blessed One, “(O Upasīva).”
Relying on "it does not exist," cross over the flood;
having abandoned sensual pleasures and abstaining from talk,
look ever toward the destruction of craving.
“Perceiving nothingness, mindful and alert”— that brahmin was already by nature an attainer of the base of nothingness, yet he did not know his support,
thinking, “This is my support. To him,
the Blessed One explained both that support and the further path to deliverance.

Having mindfully entered the attainment of the base of nothingness, and having emerged from it, he regards the mental states and mental factors arisen therein as impermanent, as suffering, and so forth—
as a disease,
as a tumor... [and so on].
As a dart...
as a calamity...
as an affliction...
... as alien, ...
as subject to dissolution, ...
as a plague, ...
As a calamity...
as a danger...
as a misfortune...
Because of its movement… because of its perishability… because of its instability…
Because it is without protection... because it is without shelter...
because it is without refuge...
As being without refuge...
as being empty... as being void...
As empty … as non-self … as a danger …
As subject to change,
as pithless,
and as the root of suffering...
from existence … from non-existence … from that which is subject to taints …
As conditioned...
as the bait of Māra...
as subject to birth...
As subject to aging … as subject to illness … as subject to death …
... from the nature of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
... from the nature of arising; ... from the nature of passing away; ...
Beholding, seeing, looking upon, contemplating, and examining [it] in terms of its gratification, its danger, and its escape.
Mindfulness is that which is mindfulness, recollection, constant recollection … [as above] … right mindfulness.
This is called mindfulness.
One who is endowed with this mindfulness … [as above] … possessed of it, is called "one who possesses mindfulness."
"Beholding nothingness, mindful.
"Upasīva," said the Blessed One.
"Upasīva," the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for veneration... [and so on] ...it is a realization-designation, namely "Bhagavā"—thus said the Blessed One to Upasīva.
"There is nothing": relying on this, cross over the flood; "there is nothing at all" refers to the attainment of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).
For what reason is there the attainment of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) with the thought, "there is nothing"?

Having mindfully entered the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*), and having emerged from it, one causes that very consciousness to cease, to disappear, and to vanish; one sees, "there is nothing.
For that reason, by relying upon, depending upon, and taking as an object the attainment of the base of nothingness with the thought, "there is nothing," [one enters it].
"Cross over, transcend, leap across, surmount, and pass beyond the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance"—
relying on "it does not exist," cross over the flood.
Having abandoned sensual desires, be detached from talk.
Regarding "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*): in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasure—sensual pleasure as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasure as defilements (*kilesakāma*).
… [as follows] … these are called sensual pleasures as objects. … [as follows] …
These are called the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*).

"Having abandoned sensual desires" means: having fully understood objective sensual desires (*vatthukāma*), and having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, brought to an end, and reduced to non-existence the defilements of sensual desire—thus, "having abandoned sensual desires."
"Abstaining from talk": here "talk" (kathaṅkathā) refers to doubt (vicikicchā).

It is doubt regarding suffering ... [and so on] ... mental paralysis, mental distress. One who is remote from, abstains from, refrains from, has emerged from, departed from, and is liberated from such talk—dwelling with a mind that has transcended its boundaries—it is in this sense that one is "abstaining from talk" ... [and so on] ...
Alternatively, he dwells with a mind that is detached, secluded, withdrawn, emerged, escaped, and liberated from the thirty-two kinds of low talk, having transcended all boundaries;
thus too, "he is abstinent from talk"—having abandoned sensual desires, he is abstinent from talk.
He beholds the destruction of craving day and night.
Craving (*taṇhā*) means craving for forms … pe … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
Night is called *natta*;
day is called *aho*.

By day and by night, behold, look closely, perceive, survey, contemplate, and examine the destruction of craving, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion; the destruction of destiny, the destruction of rebirth, the destruction of rebirth-linking, the destruction of existence,
the destruction of the round of rebirth, and the destruction of the cycle of becoming.
Behold the destruction of craving day and night!
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Perceiving nothingness, mindful, ... [the wise one] does not tremble.”
"Upasīva," said the Blessed One,
"cross over the flood by relying on 'there is not';
having abandoned sensual pleasures, be detached from talk."
“Behold the destruction of craving as the greatest good.
(Thus spoke the Venerable Upasīva: “He who is free from passion for all sensual pleasures...”
Relying on nothingness and having abandoned conceiving,
being supremely liberated through the deliverance of perception—
would he remain there, no longer following after [the world]?
“He who is free from lust for all sensual pleasures.
Regarding “all”: the word “all” (*sabbesu*) is an expression meaning in every way, entirely, completely, without remainder, and exhaustively.
Regarding “sensual pleasures” (*kāmesu*): briefly stated, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures.
There are sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements...
these are called sensual pleasures as objects...
these are called sensual pleasures as defilements.
"One who is free from lust for all sensual pleasures":

one who is free from lust, devoid of lust, with lust abandoned, with lust vomited out, with lust released, with lust relinquished, with lust given up, and with lust suppressed in regard to all sensual pleasures—
one who is thus free from lust for all sensual pleasures.
"Thus the Venerable Upasīva":
"Thus" (*icca*) is a grammatical conjunction (*padasandhi*)... [etc. ...
"Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment (*piyavacana*)... [etc. ...
"Upasīva" is the name of that brahmin... [and so on] ...the utterance—
"thus spoke the venerable Upasīva"—
is dependent upon nothingness (*ākiñcañña*), having abandoned conceiving (*maññanti*).

Having left behind, abandoned, relinquished, transcended, surpassed, and passed beyond the six lower attainments, one who is dependent upon, attached to, approached, fully approached, clung to, and intent upon the attainment of the base of nothingness—
thinking "I have left behind" while depending on nothingness—
is "supremely intent upon the liberation by perception. By "liberations by perception" are meant the seven attainments of perception.
Of those perceptions and attainments, the liberation of the base of nothingness is the foremost,
the best, the most excellent, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most sublime; he is intent upon that which is highest, foremost, best, most excellent, preeminent, supreme, and most sublime,
being resolved through the liberation of resolve, intent upon it, devoted to it, characterized by it, abundant in it, and making it his primary burden.
"Inclined toward that, leaning toward that, tending toward that, intent upon that, and dominated by that—
one is supremely intent upon liberation through perception.
Would such a person remain there without following after [the world]?"

“Does it remain?”—this is a question of doubt, a question of perplexity, a question of uncertainty, a question of indecision; [questions such as] “Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?”—thus, “does it remain?
“Therein” means in the base of nothingness.
"Anānuyāyī" means one who does not follow after, who does not depart, who does not vanish, who does not disappear, who does not decline...
[and so on]. Or alternatively: one who is not attached, who is not hateful, who is not deluded, who is not defiled—one such as this would indeed stand there without following after.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“He who is free from passion for all sensual pleasures...
(Thus spoke the Venerable Upasīva.)
Relying on the state of nothingness and having abandoned conceiving,
being supremely liberated through the deliverance by perception—
would he remain there, no longer following after [the world]?
"He who is free from passion for all sensual pleasures," said the Blessed One to Upasīva,
"and who relies on the state of nothingness, having abandoned the conceit 'I am'."
Completely liberated, supreme in the deliverance through perception,
he would abide there without following after [sensual desire].
He is one who has become free from passion for all sensual pleasures.
"In all" means: this term "in all" is an expression denoting everything in its entirety, in every way, completely, without remainder, and exhaustively.

"In sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*): briefly stated, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures—sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*). ... [as above] ...
These are called sensual pleasures of the object (*vatthukāma*) … [as above] … these are called sensual pleasures of the defilement (*kilesakāma*).
"One who is free from lust for all sensual pleasures" means one who is free from lust for all sensual pleasures … [as above] …
"Renunciation through suppression of lust" refers to one who is free from lust for all sensual pleasures.
"Upasīva, the Blessed One," [said the Blessed One].
"Upasīva," said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by name.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a designation for one who possesses reverence... [and so on] ...it is a descriptive term based on realization, namely, "the Blessed One"—thus, "Upasīva, the Blessed One."
"Dependent on nothingness, having abandoned [the lower states]" means:

having abandoned, relinquished, completely let go of, transcended, surpassed, and overcome the six lower attainments, one is dependent upon, attached to, approached, fully approached, clung to, and intent upon the attainment of the base of nothingness;
thus it is said, "dependent on nothingness, having abandoned [them], they conceive."
"Supremely devoted to the liberation by perception": the "liberations by perception" refer to the seven attainments of perception.

Among those attainments of perception, the liberation consisting of the attainment of the base of nothingness is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most sublime;
it is supreme, foremost, best, most excellent, preeminent, supreme, and most sublime.
Through liberation by resolve, he is resolved upon that; resolved upon that, resolved upon that very thing... [etc.
...having that as his dominant influence—thus, he is supremely resolved upon liberation through perception.
"He would remain there, not following after [anything else].
"He would remain" means he would remain for sixty thousand eons.
"There" means in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).
"Non-sequential" (*anānuyāyī*) means not following after, not departing, not vanishing, not disappearing,
and not declining. Alternatively, it means not being lustful, not being hateful, not being deluded, and not being defiled—
one would stand there non-sequentially.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He who is free from passion for all sensual pleasures,” (said the Blessed One to Upasīva).
Relying on nothingness and abandoning conceit,
supremely liberated through the deliverance of perception,
he would abide there, no longer following after [the world].
If he should remain there, not following after [sensual desires],
for even many years, O All-Seeing One,
then right there he would become cool and liberated.
One might expect consciousness to remain for such a person.
"If he were to remain there, not following [the stream]" means if he were to remain there for sixty thousand eons.
"There" refers to the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).
"Non-follower" means one who does not follow after, who does not depart, who does not vanish,
who does not disappear, and who does not decline. Alternatively, it means one who is not lustful, not hateful, not deluded, and not defiled—
if he should stand there as such, he is a non-follower.
"For many years, O All-Seeing One.
"For many years" means for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years,
many hundreds of thousands of years, many eons (*kalpa*), many hundreds of eons, and many thousands of eons.
For many hundreds of thousands of eons.
"All-seeing eye" (samantacakkhu): the knowledge of omniscience is called the all-seeing eye...
[and so on] ...therefore the Tathāgata is called the All-Seeing Eye.
"Even for many years, O All-Seeing One!

Right there he would become cool and liberated; the consciousness of one such as that would pass away"—this means that right there he would reach a state of coolness and remain just so forever, eternal, constant, everlasting, unchanging by nature, for all eternity.
Or else, his consciousness would pass away, be cut off, perish, vanish, and not come to be—meaning the consciousness of rebirth-linking in a future existence.

"Would he be reborn in the sense-sphere realm, the fine-material realm, or the immaterial realm?"— thus he asks about eternalism and annihilation regarding one who has attained the base of nothingness.
Or else, would he attain final nibbāna right there in the element of nibbāna without residue?
Alternatively, [the question] "Would his consciousness waver, and would rebirth-linking consciousness arise again, either in the sense-sphere realm, the fine-material realm, or the immaterial realm?
asks about both the final passing away (*parinibbāna*) and the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) of one who has been reborn in the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).
"Of such a person" means of such a one, of that kind, of one established in that way, of that sort, of one resembling that—that is, of one reborn in the base of nothingness.
Right there he would become cool and liberated; for one such as that, consciousness would pass away.
Therefore that brahmin said:
"If he were to remain there, not subject to further wandering..."
“Even for many years, O All-Seeing One,
he would remain right there, cooled and liberated;
yet for one such as that, consciousness would still pass away.”
"Just as a flame cast by the force of the wind goes out and can no longer be reckoned," said the Blessed One, "O Upasīva."
Thus the sage, liberated from the group of names,
reaches his goal and does not enter into reckoning.
"As a flame cast by the force of the wind"— here "flame" refers to the crest of a mass of fire.
There are eastern winds, western winds, northern winds, southern winds; winds with dust, winds without dust;
cold winds, hot winds; slight winds, intense winds; *verambha* winds, wing-winds, garuḍa-winds, palm-leaf winds, and fanning winds.
"Cast by the force of the wind" means cast, tossed up, driven, pushed away, checked, or obstructed by the force of the wind—
just as a flame is cast by the force of the wind.
"Upasīva," said the Blessed One.
“Upasīva,” said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by name.
“Blessed One” (bhagavā) is a term of respect... [and so on] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, “the Blessed One”—thus says the Blessed One: “Upasīva.”
"It goes to its end; it does not enter into reckoning.
"It goes to its end" means it goes to its end, it reaches its end, it goes to its end, it ceases, it subsides, it becomes tranquil.
"It does not enter into reckoning" means it does not enter into reckoning, it does not enter into description, it does not enter into calculation, it does not enter into designation.
It does not go to the thought, "I have gone to the eastern direction, or the western direction, or the northern direction, or the southern direction;
or I have gone upwards, or downwards, or across, or to the intermediate directions.
There is no cause, no condition, no reason by which it could be reckoned as such.
"It passes away and does not enter into reckoning;
thus the sage is liberated from the mental body.
Here, "thus" (*evaṃ*) serves as the application of the simile.
“Muni”: *mone* (silence) is said to be knowledge … [as before] … having transcended the net of attachments, he is a muni.
“Liberated from the mental body (*nāmakāya*): that muni was already liberated from the physical body (*rūpakāya*) by his very nature;
it was abandoned through the abandonment of suppression by means of transcendence of its constituent parts (*tadaṅga*).
By coming to this sage, the four noble paths have been attained by you.
Because the four noble paths have been attained, both the mental body and the physical body have been fully understood.

Because both the mental body and the physical body have been fully understood, you are liberated from the mental body and the physical body—liberated, utterly liberated, through the liberation that is absolute non-clinging.
Thus the sage, liberated from the group of names, passes away into the ultimate goal; he does not enter into conceptualization.
"He passes away into the ultimate goal" means that he attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue.

He does not enter into reckoning; one who has attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue does not enter into reckoning, does not enter into description, does not enter into calculation, and does not enter into designation—whether as a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, or a worker;
whether as a householder or one gone forth; whether as a deva or a human; whether as one possessing form or formless; whether as percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.
There is no cause, no condition, and no reason by which he could be brought into reckoning.
It goes to its end and can no longer be reckoned.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Just as a flame cast by the force of the wind, ...goes to its end and can no longer be reckoned."
(“Upasīva,” said the Blessed One,) “He passes away and cannot be reckoned;
thus the sage, liberated from the group of names.”
"It goes to its end and cannot be reckoned.
Has it gone to its end, or does it not exist,
or is it indeed forever healthy?
Please explain this well to me, O Sage, for this Dhamma is known to you.
Has he who has set out [from the world] ceased to exist? Or does he not exist? Has he who has set out perished, been cut off, and utterly destroyed?
"Has he set out for the goal, or does he not exist?
Or rather, is he healthy forever? Or is he permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, remaining exactly as he is for all eternity?"—thus, "Is he indeed healthy forever?"
"Please explain that well to me, O Sage.
"That" refers to what I ask, what I entreat, what I beseech, and what I inspire with confidence.
"Sage" (muni): wisdom is called *mona*... [as far as] ...having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a sage.
"Please explain well" means: "Please declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and make manifest"—O Sage, please explain that well to me.
For this Dhamma has been known by you; for this Dhamma has been known, weighed, scrutinized, made clear, and fully realized by you.
For this Dhamma is known by him. Therefore that brahmin said:
"Has he set out [into the beyond], or does he not exist?"
Or is one indeed free from illness for all eternity?
O Sage, please explain this well to me,
for this Dhamma is known to you.
"There is no measure for one who has gone to cessation," said the Blessed One to Upasīva,
"for that by which they might describe him does not exist for him."
When all phenomena have been eradicated, all paths of speech are also eradicated. For one who has gone to cessation, there is no measure;
that is, for one who has gone to cessation and is fully extinguished in the Nibbāna-element without remainder.
There is no measure of form, no measure of feeling, no measure of perception, no measure of volitional formations,
and no measure of consciousness; it does not exist, is not found, and is not obtained— it has been abandoned,
cut off, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising again, burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
“There is no measure for one who has gone to rest.
“Upasīva,” said the Blessed One—“Upasīva,” the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
“Blessed One” (bhagavā) is a term of respect... [and so on] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, “the Blessed One.”
"Upasīva," said the Blessed One,
"that by which they might speak of him does not exist for him—
that by which they might speak of him through lust, through hatred, through delusion, through conceit, through views, or through agitation."
Whatever doubts they might speak of, whatever underlying tendencies they might speak of—
whether as "lustful," "hateful," "deluded," "bound," "clinging," "distracted," "gone astray," or "firmly rooted"— those volitional formations have been abandoned.
Because those volitional formations have been abandoned, there is no destination by which they could speak of him.
Whether one is called a denizen of hell, or an animal, or a being in the realm of ghosts, or a human, or a deva;

or one who has form, or one who is formless; or one who possesses perception, or one who is non-percipient, or one who is neither percipient nor non-percipient—there is no cause, there is no condition, there is no reason by which they might say, speak, utter, illuminate, or express [such things].
That by which they might describe him does not exist for him.

"When all phenomena have been eradicated" means: when all phenomena—meaning all aggregates (*khandha*), all bases (*āyatana*), all elements (*dhātu*), all destinations (*gati*), all rebirths (*upapatti*), all re-linkings (*paṭisandhi*), and all states of existence (*bhava*)—have been eradicated.
When all rounds of existence and all cycles have been eroded, thoroughly eroded, uprooted, thoroughly uprooted, torn out, thoroughly torn out,
abandoned, cut off, stilled, calmed, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt away by the fire of knowledge— this is what it means.
"When all phenomena have been eradicated, even the paths of speech are eradicated.
Here, "paths of speech" refers to the defilements (*kilesa*), the aggregates (*khandha*), and volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).

For him, both the speeches and the paths of speech, as well as the designations (*adhivacana*) and the paths of designation, and the language (*nirutti*) and the paths of language, [are all eradicated].
Concepts, modes of conceptualization, and paths of conceptualization have been uprooted, thoroughly uprooted, drawn out, thoroughly drawn out, torn away, thoroughly torn away,
abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed; rendered incapable of arising and consumed by the fire of knowledge—
all paths of discourse have been thoroughly uprooted.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“There is no measure for one who has gone to rest,” (said the Blessed One to Upasīva).
That by which they might speak of him does not exist for him;
when all phenomena have been eradicated,
all paths of speech are also eradicated.
At the conclusion of that verse, those who had been with the brahmin...
[and so on] ...who were sitting with palms joined in reverence, said:
"Venerable sir, the Blessed One is our teacher; I am his disciple."
The sixth exposition: The Questions of the Young Brahmin Upasīva.
